case_study_insert.main_stem: Sable Ridge Agribusiness (SRA) is a public limited company in the grain-milling sector, employing a workforce of 74. Founded in 1998 by Isobel Ridge, it supplies flour and animal feed to bakeries and farms and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. SRA plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new silo and automated milling line with biodegradable packaging, financed by a $700,000 bank loan and a $500,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $330,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.40 a unit and a selling price of $13.40, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. SRA faces two problems: a skills gap on the new mill and grain waste has reached 4%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Waste Report — Q2 2025: The mill processed 30,000 sacks last quarter at a defect rate of 2.2%, down from 3.5% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 33 to 17 per month. Average delivery time is 5.2 days. A survey of 610 buyers found that 63% preferred biodegradable packaging and 49% would pay up to $0.55 more. A skills audit shows 22 of 74 staff need on-the-job training on the new mill; off-the-job training at the college costs $950 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Sable Ridge Agribusiness as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (February 2027): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, increasing interest on SRA's variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $13.40 to $14.14 per hour from April 2026, increasing the wage bill. (3) Wholesale fertiliser, fuel and packaging costs have risen 13.2% year-on-year, and food-input inflation is 8.3%, while consumer spending on bakery products grew 2.6%.

questions.question_text: SRA plans to fund part of its milling expansion with a $700,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for SRA of using a share issue rather than the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue, here $500,000, raises equity that does not have to be repaid and carries no compulsory interest, unlike the $700,000 bank loan. For a public limited company with $330,000 of fixed costs, this lowers the risk of default if grain demand weakens and leaves cash flow freer while the $1,200,000 mill is commissioned.

Point 2: Equity from shareholders can fund a larger, long-term asset such as the new silo without the collateral and covenants a bank would demand, and it strengthens the balance sheet. The newly issued shares also spread ownership beyond founder Isobel Ridge, giving SRA access to more capital for future expansion, which is useful as it faces a 5.5% wage rise and 13.2% input inflation at the same time.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to SRA's financing, risk and costs.

questions.question_text: SRA is launching biodegradable packaging for its flour range. Consider national television advertising, trade fairs and exhibitions, or social media influencer marketing. Which should SRA choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: TV would quickly build awareness of the biodegradable packaging among all buyers of flour and animal feed. However, airtime is very expensive for a 74-employee plc already funding a $1,200,000 mill, and much of the mass audience buys neither flour nor feed, so most of the spend would miss SRA's industrial and bakery customers.

Trade fairs and exhibitions: These put SRA's flour and feed directly in front of bakery and farm buyers, allowing demonstrations of the biodegradable packaging and immediate order-taking — a strong fit for business-to-business sales of 30,000 sacks a quarter. They are cheaper than television and provide competitor intelligence. Limits are that they occur only occasionally and require staff time, so they cannot maintain continuous awareness between events.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and baking influencers could reach the 63% of 610 surveyed buyers who prefer biodegradable packaging and the 49% who would pay up to $0.55 more, with measurable engagement at low cost per contact. The content can run continuously and nationally. It depends on influencer credibility and reaches final consumers more than the bakeries and farms that actually place the orders, so conversion may be slower.

Recommendation: SRA should choose trade fairs and exhibitions as the primary channel. They reach the exact business buyers who place the 30,000-sack quarterly orders and suit a 74-staff agribusiness funding a $1,200,000 expansion; television is rejected as costly and untargeted at mass consumers, and influencer marketing is rejected as better suited to end buyers than to the bakery and farm customers SRA supplies. SRA can use social media as a low-cost supplement.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to SRA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in SRA's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discusses all three options in SRA's context and recommends trade fairs with clear reasons for rejecting television and influencers.

questions.question_text: SRA faces a skills gap on the new mill and grain waste of 4%. Explain two benefits for SRA of using autocratic leadership to improve output and reduce waste.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets SRA's managers impose clear operating rules on the new mill, which directly addresses the 4% grain waste and the 2.2% defect rate by standardising how the 74 staff run the equipment. In a hierarchical structure, decisive instructions cut confusion and get the $1,200,000 investment productive quickly, protecting the 120,000-unit plan.

Point 2: Central control also allows SRA to direct the $950-per-employee off-the-job training budget to the 22 staff with the skills gap, choosing exactly who needs it rather than leaving selection to chance. Faster decisions can close the gap before output suffers, defending the $6.00 contribution per unit against 13.2% input inflation and helping SRA meet bakery and farm delivery schedules despite the $330,000 of fixed costs.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for development linked to SRA's skills gap, waste, defect rate and training.

questions.question_text: SRA must train 22 staff on the new mill. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the college. Which should SRA choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Instruction at the mill is specific to SRA's own equipment and quality checks, costs no fees, and keeps the 22 staff productive while learning, protecting the 30,000-sack quarterly output and the effort to cut the 2.2% defect rate. Its weaknesses are that supervisors training staff divert effort from their own work, bad habits may be copied, and there is no formal certificate for large bakery customers.

Off-the-job training: The college course at $950 per employee gives structured, current skills and a recognised qualification for all 22 staff, costing $20,900 — small beside the $1,200,000 mill. However, it removes staff from the line during a skills gap, cutting short-term output, and generic content may not match SRA's mill settings, so on-site coaching would still follow.

Decision: SRA should choose on-the-job training as the core approach, with college courses for a handful of senior operators. It is cheaper, mill-specific and avoids losing output while the skills gap is open and waste is 4%; full off-the-job training is rejected because $20,900 and twenty-two absences would jeopardise bakery and farm deliveries, and the qualification can be added once the mill runs smoothly.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with limited application to SRA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in SRA's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both methods in SRA's context with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SRA's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 55,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety against 120,000-unit output; pricing against $330,000 fixed costs; loan and share-issue feasibility for the $1,200,000 mill; and unit-cost benchmarking at $10.15 to reduce 4% waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate answer in each calculation; 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $330,000 ÷ ($13.40 − $7.40) = $330,000 ÷ $6.00 = 55,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 55,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $13.40 − $7.40 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SRA's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 55,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 120,000 units, a margin of safety of 65,000 units, to gauge how far flour and feed demand could fall before the new mill loses money.
2. Contribution per unit of $6.00 lets SRA test a customer discount: a $0.55 cut would leave $5.45, showing the extra volume needed to cover $330,000 of fixed costs.
3. Knowing contribution and fixed costs helps check that 120,000 units generate enough to service the $700,000 bank loan and justify the $500,000 share issue behind the $1,200,000 mill.
4. Unit cost of $10.15 ($330,000 ÷ 120,000 units + $7.40) gives a benchmark to isolate the 4% grain waste and 2.2% defect rate, supporting supplier negotiations amid 13.2% input inflation.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SRA's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SRA's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.30 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.85 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.10 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $126,000 inventories + $168,000 trade receivables + $70,000 cash = $364,000; 2025 current assets = $104,000 + $206,000 + $80,000 = $390,000. Dividing by current liabilities of $280,000 and $260,000 gives 1.30 and 1.50. Excluding inventories, $238,000 ÷ $280,000 = 0.85 in 2024 and $286,000 ÷ $260,000 = 1.10 in 2025.

Evaluation: Liquidity has clearly improved. The broader measure rose from 1.30 to 1.50 as current liabilities fell from $280,000 to $260,000 and current assets rose to $390,000. The stricter measure improved from 0.85 to 1.10, helped by inventories falling from $126,000 to $104,000, so SRA no longer needs to sell grain stocks to cover short-term debts — important while it services a $700,000 bank loan and spends $1,200,000 on the mill. However, trade receivables rose from $168,000 to $206,000, tying up cash that could fund the 5.5% wage rise; if bakery and farm customers pay late, the improvement could unwind.

Conclusion: SRA's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher and the stricter measure now exceeds 1 without relying on inventories. The key residual risk is rising receivables, so SRA should tighten credit control before drawing further on the $700,000 loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States figures with little or no accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates both ratios for both years accurately with some contextual analysis.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations plus detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SRA of using biodegradable packaging for its flour range.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Biodegradable packaging appeals to the 63% of 610 surveyed buyers who prefer it and the 49% who would pay up to $0.55 more, helping SRA protect the $6.00 contribution per unit as fertiliser, fuel and packaging costs rise 13.2%. It also supports the brand with bakeries and farms supplied by the $1,200,000 mill.

Disadvantage: Biodegradable materials usually cost more than standard sacks, which would raise the $7.40 variable cost per unit unless the full $0.55 premium is obtained. If the material is less durable in storage it could worsen the 4% grain waste and the 2.2% defect rate, adding cost to the 120,000-unit output just as SRA is trying to close its skills gap.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using SRA's research, costs and waste data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 13.2% rise in input costs will affect SRA. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): SRA has a $700,000 bank loan, and if it is variable-rate the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% × $700,000 = $5,250 (0.0075 × $700,000). That is noticeable but modest beside $330,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan were fixed-rate the charge would be zero. Higher rates may also dampen consumer spending on bakery products and raise future borrowing costs, but SRA can cap the risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $14.14 per hour): With a workforce of 74 in milling and packing, this raises the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so no annual total can be honestly invented; the sound test is productivity — 120,000 units ÷ 74 staff is about 1,622 units per worker, so the rise is manageable only if productivity holds or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost erodes the $6.00 contribution.

Input cost inflation (13.2% fertiliser, fuel and packaging): The insert never decomposes the $7.40 variable cost, so only a bound is defensible — if the whole variable cost rose 13.2% it would add 13.2% × $7.40 = $0.98 per unit, and at 120,000 units that is about $117,300 a year. Even a partial pass-through would cut contribution sharply, and 8.3% food-input inflation may limit SRA's ability to pass costs to bakeries.

Conclusion: The 13.2% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It repeats across all 120,000 units and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution that supports the $1,200,000 mill, whereas the interest rise costs at most about $5,250 and the wage rise can partly be offset by productivity.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to SRA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on SRA's costs, financing or revenue in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes with a justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
